**Main workflow**

**Input datasets**

detailed\_monitoring\_plots\_2017\_2026\_est.csv – already filtered dataset queried and exported from this [link](https://kese.envir.ee/parameterValue1?parameter=N100003633&parameter=N100003427&parameter=N100005797&parameter=N100005419&parameter=N100005416&status=VALID&status=VERIFIED&status=EXCEPT&validFrom=Tue%20Jan%2001%202019%2000:00:00%20GMT%200200%20\(Ida-Euroopa%20standardaeg\)&validTo=Wed%20Oct%2014%202026%2000:00:00%20GMT%200300%20\(Ida-Euroopa%20suveaeg\)&program=PR0032) 7723 kb

10 Sentinel-2 indices (NDVI, EVI, LAI, SAVI, FVC, GNDVI, NDWI, BSI, NDMI and alpha diversity) and one Sentinel-1 index (RVI) extracted from public catalogue https://metadata.geokuup.ee/stac/web/browse/catalog/estonia

**1\. Data preparation (data\_preparation\_1.ipynb)**

Forest habitat monitoring data from 2017–2026 were processed to create a spatial reference dataset. Steps:

1.  Selected monitoring plots with a 20 m observation radius and transformed indicator records into one row per plot.
2.  Corrected coordinates, excluded conflicting habitat labels, and retained the latest observation at duplicate locations.
3.  Extracted Natura 2000 forest habitat codes and created 20 m radius circular polygons (EPSG:3301).
4.  Prepared and combined Natura 2000 inventory polygon datasets for potential future use. Only monitoring plots were selected for the initial model.
5.  Retained observations from 1 June 2017 onward and assigned each plot a corresponding remote sensing year to be used. For observations in January–August, the previous year's summer imagery was selected (except 2017 for which 2016 remote sensing data was not available). Observations from September 2025 onward until november 2026 were assigned 2025 imagery.
6.  Exported the prepared monitoring plots and relevant map-sheet selections as GeoPackage files.

**2\. Raster data extraction (raster\_data\_extraction\_2.ipynb)**

Remote sensing variables were extracted from the University of Tartu's geokuup.ee cloud-optimized GeoTIFF datasets.

1.  Selected 10 Sentinel-2 indices (NDVI, EVI, LAI, SAVI, FVC, GNDVI, NDWI, BSI, NDMI and alpha diversity) and one Sentinel-1 index (RVI).
2.  Used summer (June–August) raster products corresponding to each plot's assigned remote sensing year.
3.  Extracted raster pixels intersecting each 20 m monitoring plot using Rasterio, including boundary-touching pixels (all\_touched=True).
4.  Excluded NoData and non-finite values, and multiplied valid pixel values by 0.001 to restore the original scale.
5.  Calculated the mean, median and number of valid pixels separately for each index and monitoring plot.
6.  Summarized missing values and pixel counts, then exported the resulting spatial dataset with remote sensing predictors to GeoPackage.

**3\. Spatial train-test split (data\_preparation\_3.ipynb)**

The script prepares forest habitat monitoring plots for machine learning by dividing observations into training and test sets.

1.  Load monitoring plots containing Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 indices and Natura 2000 habitat inventory polygons. Select 10 forest habitat types from the inventory dataset.
2.  Join monitoring plots with intersecting Natura inventory polygons, retaining polygon identifiers, habitat types and inventory dates. Where multiple inventory polygons intersect a plot, retain the polygon with the most recent inventory date.
3.  Cluster monitoring plot centroids using DBSCAN with a 1 km distance threshold. Merge clusters connected through the same Natura inventory polygon to prevent observations associated with one polygon from being divided between training and test datasets.
4.  Generate 3,000 candidate group-based splits (AI suggestion, could be analysed further) using GroupShuffleSplit, targeting approximately 80% training and 20% test observations. Select the split that minimizes deviations from the target test proportion and differences in habitat type and remote sensing year distributions between datasets.
5.  Compare habitat type and remote sensing year distributions across training and test datasets. Verify that no spatial group or matched Natura inventory polygon occurs in both datasets.
6.  Export monitoring plot polygons with their original attributes, inventory information, spatial group identifiers and train/test labels to GeoPackage. Create an additional centroid layer and visualize the spatial distribution of training and test observations across Estonia.

Limitations are as follows: The 1 km clustering threshold has not been empirically validated against spatial autocorrelation. Class proportions are balanced approximately rather than guaranteed, and rare habitat types may have too few test observations for reliable class-specific accuracy assessment.

**4\. Random Forest habitat-type model (random\_forest\_model\_4.ipynb)**

The model predicts monitoring-plot `habitat_code` for the ten forest habitat classes from the mean and median Sentinel index values extracted for each plot. Unlabeled observations and the `0` (“0 elupaigatüüp”) label are excluded. It uses the spatial train/test labels created in step 3 rather than making a new random split. Missing predictor values are median-imputed within a scikit-learn pipeline, so imputation is fitted on training data only. The Random Forest uses balanced class weights to account for uneven class frequencies. Test accuracy, balanced accuracy, macro F1, per-class results, and a confusion matrix are reported. The fitted pipeline and held-out predictions are saved under `working/`.

No whole-raster min-max normalization is applied: the extraction notebook already converts the stored integer index values using the catalog scale factor. The model's performance should be treated as an initial baseline, especially for rare habitat classes.

***Separate Test to Analyse Which Areas Have Enough Reference Data***

The aim was to identify suitable pilot areas for modelling Natura 2000 forest habitat types or structural preservation.

Two reference datasets are used: forest monitoring plots (20 m radius) and Natura habitat inventory polygons. Duplicate monitoring locations and invalid records are removed. Each inventory polygon is represented by one point located at least 20 m from its boundary.

Estonia was divided into overlapping **40 × 40 km candidate areas**, shifted by 10 km. Each area was evaluated using two potential target variables:

-   **Habitat type:** Number and distribution of different habitat classes.
-   **Structural preservation:** Distribution of preservation classes (I, II, III) within individual habitat types.

A class was considered sufficiently represented if it contained at least **30 reference observations distributed across three or more 10 × 10 km blocks**.

Candidate areas were ranked according to class representation, spatial distribution and monitoring plot availability.

Finally, class distributions were compared between the best pilot areas and all of Estonia. An illustrative 80% training / 20% testing split was calculated to assess sample sizes.

**Preparation of Natura Forest Habitat Reference Data to Test Possible Folding**

Monitoring and inventory data preparation for later remote-sensing modelling was tested. Records from 20 m radius monitoring plots were cleaned, spatially separated training and evaluation groups are created, and optional additional points can be sampled from inside habitat inventory polygons.

Records from KESE forest habitat monitoring were selected when a 20 m plot radius is explicitly recorded. As each indicator is stored in a separate CSV row, the indicators belonging to one observation were combined into a single record. Habitat type was taken from the *Elupaigatüüp (LD)* field. Habitat codes and assessment categories were standardised, while the original values were retained just in case. The reversed easting and northing fields in the source file were corrected, and observations with invalid coordinates were separated. Observations were flagged according to whether they fall within 2017–2026. A circular polygon with a 20 m radius was also created around each valid monitoring centre.

Natura habitat inventory polygons were loaded if the inventory file is available. Their geometries were transformed to EPSG:3301, invalid geometries were repaired, and unusable polygons were excluded. Relevant field names and assessment codes were standardised while retaining the original values. An inventory assessment describes the entire polygon, rather than a measured condition at one specific point.

Monitoring plots were grouped into 10 × 10 km spatial blocks. Five folds were created using StratifiedGroupKFold, which kept plots from the same block together and attempted to balance the selected assessment classes. By default, the balance was based on structural preservation. Fold 0 is reserved for final testing, while folds 1–4 are used for training and spatial cross-validation.

Where monitoring plots overlapped inventory polygons, their fold assignments were coordinated. Polygons associated with plots from different blocks or folds, together with the affected monitoring plots, were flagged for possible exclusion. Training observations less than 1 km from final test observations were also flagged for exclusion, but the records are retained just in case. A similar distance buffer can be applied during cross-validation. These steps were created to guarantee that training and testiong would be done with plots not too cxlose to each ohter, because this can cause overfitting in the end

Up to six spatially distributed points could be generated within each eligible inventory polygon (number of points can be decided in diferent way if needed). Where possible, points can be placed at least 20 m inside the polygon boundary and at least 60 m apart. Each point inherits the polygon assessment and can be marked as inventory\_weak, because it is not an independent field observation. Each point receives a weight of 1 / number of points in its polygon, so the total weight of one polygon is one, regardless of the number of sampled points. These points are intended as optional additional training data, not as the main accuracy test. This step described in this paragraph was not done at the moment, because it is unclear if extra data is needed and if it is helpful.

GeoPackage files were exported for monitoring centres, 20 m monitoring circles, inventory polygons, optional sample points, and spatial blocks. CSV summaries describe fold assignments, assessment classes, observation years, and quality checks. Remote-sensing predictors were not calculated and models were not trained or evaluated at this stage. The 10 km block size and 1 km buffer were initial choices whose suitability can be decided upon.

monitoring\_centres – Point locations representing the centres of 20 m radius Natura forest habitat monitoring plots. Each point contains the monitoring results, including habitat type and condition assessments.

monitoring\_plots\_20m – Circular polygons with a 20 m radius (approximately 1,257 m²), created around the monitoring centres. They represent the area assessed during field monitoring and can be used to extract local remote-sensing characteristics.

spatial\_groups – describe blockids and corresponding fold ids.

These folds were stratified based on structural preservation, so it is clear that other classifications representability is not as balanced across folds. So folding would need to be done again for other features if needed. Also we have probably not enough data without inventories, so inventory data might be needed. Or bigger folds created. It can be seen that there are not many exclusions, but further exploration is needed to be sure that close monitoring plots would not fall into separate folds.
